question.text:
A body travels along a rectilinear path with an acceleration that changes over time as described below. If the body begins its motion from rest at t = 0 s, sketch the corresponding velocity-time graph from t = 0 s to t = 6 s:
• For 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s, acceleration a = +2 m/s²
• For 2 s < t ≤ 4 s, acceleration a = 0 m/s²
• For 4 s < t ≤ 6 s, acceleration a = −4 m/s²
conditions: starts from rest (v = 0 at t = 0 s)
constant acceleration of +2 m/s² from t = 0 to 2 s
zero acceleration from t = 2 to 4 s
constant acceleration of −4 m/s² from t = 4 to 6 s

figure.description: An acceleration versus time (a-t) plot where acceleration is plotted on the vertical axis in m/s² and time is on the horizontal axis in seconds. The graph has three piecewise horizontal segments: a segment at a = +2 m/s² spanning from t = 0 s to 2 s, a segment along the time axis at a = 0 m/s² from t = 2 s to 4 s, and a segment at a = −4 m/s² extending from t = 4 s to 6 s.

solution.approach: Add the change in velocity from each interval of the a-t graph one after another, starting from v = 0, to build up the v-t graph.

steps.text: From t = 0 to 2 s, acceleration is a constant +2 m/s², so velocity rises in a straight line.
From t = 2 to 4 s, acceleration is 0, so velocity stays constant.
From t = 4 to 6 s, acceleration is a constant −4 m/s², so velocity falls in a straight line.
Find when the falling line crosses zero between t = 4 s and t = 6 s.

final_answer.value: The v-t graph rises in a straight line from (0, 0) to (2 s, 4 m/s), stays flat at 4 m/s from 2 s to 4 s, then falls in a straight line through (5 s, 0) down to (6 s, −4 m/s).

common_mistakes.text: Treating the flat 0 m/s² interval as zero velocity instead of constant velocity makes the graph drop to zero between 2 s and 4 s.
Reading the crossing point as t = 4 s, the start of deceleration, instead of solving for where v actually reaches zero, misses that it happens at t = 5 s.
